Rheumatology · published research

Raynaud syndrome

A 15-person crossover trial found lower attack intensity during laser treatment than placebo but no significant reduction in attack frequency. Another controlled study reported improvement in symptoms, while thermographic findings and response duration were inconsistent.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 15-person crossover trial found lower attack intensity during laser treatment than placebo but no significant reduction in attack frequency. Another controlled study reported improvement in symptoms, while thermographic findings and response duration were inconsistent.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Circulation > Raynaud syndrome category contains five human publications: three randomized controlled or crossover reports and two uncontrolled studies. Two pairs of papers come from recurring research groups, and cohort independence is not fully documented. There are no animal or laboratory records in this category.

Human and clinical evidence

In a 15-person randomized crossover trial, low-level laser therapy reduced attack intensity compared with placebo but did not significantly change attack frequency; the effect did not carry over after treatment stopped (Hirschl et al. 2002). A later 47-person placebo-controlled trial also reported lower attack intensity, but clinical and thermographic outcomes were not uniformly different from placebo (al-Awami et al. 2004). Another 48-person trial reported symptom improvement, but came from the same research group as the earlier Hirschl paper (Hirschl et al. 2004). Two uncontrolled reports cannot separate treatment effects from natural variation, expectation, or seasonal changes.

Animal evidence

No animal experiment is listed for this indication.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory or ex-vivo study is listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The reports apply low-level laser treatment to patients with primary or secondary Raynaud phenomenon, using repeated sessions over several weeks. Study schedules and measured outcomes differ. Wavelength describes the light's color band and can affect tissue interaction, but the records do not establish a common effective clinical protocol.

Interpretation

The controlled evidence supports a possible short-term reduction in attack intensity in some patients. Attack frequency, warming measures, durability, and independent replication are less certain. Better trials should stratify primary and secondary disease and use standardized symptom diaries and cold-challenge outcomes.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for reduced attack intensity during laser treatment in small placebo-controlled studies Very low for attack frequency, thermographic change, or lasting benefit
Publications and records5 unique titles (exact Circulation > Raynaud syndrome)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Three small controlled studies and two uncontrolled reports examine Raynaud symptoms. Attack intensity improved in some trials, but attack frequency and thermographic responses were inconsistent, and both active and placebo groups sometimes improved. Independent trials should use validated attack diaries and longer follow-up.
